title: Rök runestone (Ög 136), Östergötland, c. 800: the cipher runes checked

documents.shelfmark: Rök runestone, Rök church, Östergötland, Sweden; Rundata Ög 136
documents.route: carver Varinn -> readers of the stone

plaintext.source: Rundata Ög 136 and Wessén, Runstenen vid Rök (1958); the cipher runes were first read by Sophus Bugge (1878).

transcription.source: English Wikipedia 'Rök runestone' Unicode section (CC BY-SA 4.0), after Rundata Ög 136; transcription.txt
transcription.notes: No image of the stone was read here; the rune string is the published transcription. Lost runes in the penultimate Younger-futhark line are marked - or ... in the source.

system.summary: A runic inscription that mixes plain 16-rune Younger Futhark with three cipher devices: twig-rune coordinates (aett:position), a one-step shift along the futhark row, and an Elder Futhark substitution that merges voiced and unvoiced consonants.
system.notes: The coordinate cipher is the aett-and-position (twig-rune) scheme with the aett counted from the right; the shift cipher moves each rune one place back in the 16-rune row; the Elder passage is not a shift (k and g share one rune, as do t and d, and i has three).

conditions.human_role: Set the goal; asked twice for the cipher layers to be derived rather than copied, and then for the write-up.
tools: WebFetch of English Wikipedia for the transcription

solution.what: Web search and Wikipedia: the cipher runes of Rök are read and printed in Rundata Ög 136; only the meaning is disputed.

Fetched the wikitext of English Wikipedia's Rök runestone article for the full Unicode rune string, the transliteration with ciphers resolved, the Old East Norse normalisation and the English translation.
Twig-rune coordinates [a:b]: tested the aett-from-the-right table against all 11 distinct codes on the stone; all agree with the stone's own resolutions.
Shift cipher: tried all 16 shifts along the 16-rune row on the 24-rune string and scored each by 4-grams shared with the stone's own cleartext; shift +1 wins, giving sakum mukmini uaim si burin niþ.
The same search on the 8-rune string was uninformative (too short); +1 applied from the 24-rune result gives knuą knat.

Elder Futhark passage: the stone's own cleartext contains sakum mukmini þat, which opens the passage; the 14 runes fix 11 rune values (s,a,k/g,u,m,i,n,þ,t/d and the two forms of u and i); unchanged runes read as themselves; the rest reads huaʀ i k/gult/d k/ga uaʀi k/gult/d int/d t/d k/guąnaʀ husli.
Glyph-to-letter comparison of the main text with the published transliteration: 98.84% sequence similarity; the differences are bind-runes and editorial brackets.
The lost runes of the line beginning nuk m--- have no key to recover and were not filled in.

outcome.method_basis: Bugge (1878), Wessén (1958) and Rundata Ög 136 published the cipher readings; here the published coordinate table, a searched shift key and a crib-fixed Elder substitution were checked against the published transcription and each agrees with the published resolution.
outcome.fraction_read_source: decode_layers.py / layers_report.txt: every intact cipher rune in the coordinate, shift and Elder layers decodes (lost runes excluded)
outcome.notes: Fully derived keys, no new reading. The voiced/unvoiced choice in the Elder passage (k/g, t/d) is a spelling question of the Younger-futhark orthography, not part of the key. Damaged runes in the line beginning nuk m--- are lost on the stone. Meaning of the inscription remains debated.

credits.note: Standard reading of the cipher runes (known here through Rundata and Wikipedia, not consulted directly), building on Bugge (1878)

texts.label: Rök runestone, full inscription
texts.summary: The Rök stone, carved c. 800 by Varinn in memory of his dead son Vámóðr, asks a series of riddle-like questions about two war-booties, Theodoric, Gunnr's horse and twenty kings, and closes by invoking Thor. The cipher runes carry the final stretches, from the Ingold passage on.
